transcript.reader:
Let me check I have it before I test it: your central claim is that trading a MAC-10 for cocaine is "use" of the firearm under §924(c)(1), because "use" takes its ordinary meaning of converting a thing to one's service, and §924(d)(3) applies the same word to guns intended to be sold or transferred as goods — is that a fair version of the claim, and is it meant to answer *what counts as "use" under this rule*, over exactly what range of cases?

Take that one part — "use" means any converting to one's service — and give me both halves of a poke: name one change to the world that your reading says *would* still count as "use" during and in relation to a drug crime, and one it says would *not*.
transcript.author:
Yes—fair, with one refinement. My claim is not that “use” is infinitely elastic; it is that “use” carries its ordinary broad sense, and §924(d)(3)’s gun-commerce offenses confirm that trading is a use. But “use” alone is not the rule: it must be during and in relation to a drug crime. That second requirement is the limiting principle. So the range is any employment of a gun that has a purpose or effect with respect to the drug offense—barter, collateral, bludgeon, etc.—not merely coincidental possession or wholly innocent handling.

Would still count: A defendant, unable to sell his gun, uses it as collateral to secure a drug debt, with the gun to be returned when the debt is paid. That converts the gun to service in the drug crime and facilitates it; under my reading, it counts.

Would not count: A defendant at a drug deal scratches his head with the barrel of a gun. He has “used” the gun in the dictionary sense, but the use has no purpose or effect with respect to the drug crime, so it is not “in relation to” it and §924(c)(1) is not triggered. That is the distinction the dissent overlooks.

transcript.reader:
Two swaps, one per part.

First, the central part. Hand you the tool: give me a *different* reading of "uses a firearm" in §924(c)(1) — a near neighbour a fair person might really have proposed, not a straw man — that would work just as well for the case. If you can, what made you pick yours? If you cannot, what exactly stops you?

Second, the §924(d)(3) crutch. Congress used "involved in" alongside "intended to be used" elsewhere in §924(d)(1). Swap your part for that neighbour: suppose the gun-commerce offenses had been listed under the "involved in" phrase rather than the "intended to be used" phrase — would your inference that §924(c)(1) reaches barter still stand, or does the whole cross-reference rest on that particular word choice?
transcript.author:
**Part one.** I have to be candid: the genuine near-neighbour is Justice Scalia's contextual reading — "uses a firearm" ordinarily means uses it as a weapon. It is a real reading, honestly argued, but it decides the case *the other way*, so it does not "work just as well" for this outcome. The only same-result alternative I can offer is not a reading of "use" at all: affirmance on "carrying," since Smith kept the MAC-10 in a bag on his person. But I expressly declined that ground because the indictment charged only "use." What stops me from supplying a different same-result reading of "use" is that the interpretive space is close to binary on these facts: either employment as commodity counts or it does not. A narrower reading loses the case; a broader one adds nothing. I chose mine because the ordinary meaning of "use" is broad — "to convert to one's service" — and §924(d) supplied a textual twin for the commodity sense.

**Part two.** No — as written, it would not stand. That inference rests entirely on Congress' word choice. I myself reasoned that Congress used "involved in" for §922(a)(6) precisely because a false statement is not "use" even under the broadest definition. If the sale and export offenses had been listed under "involved in," Congress would be signalling that commodity dealings are *not* "use" but merely involvement — the opposite inference. The parallel would collapse, and the dissent's contextual argument would gain real force. I would be left with ordinary meaning alone, which is thinner ground.

transcript.reader:
Add one job first. Your reading now needs "carries a firearm" to say something of its own: Smith had the MAC-10 in a gun bag on his person, so on your account he both used it and carried it. Name the case where "uses" and "carries" come apart under your reading, and tell me which rival readings that new job kills — or whether it kills none.

Now pull two of your parts against each other. Push "use" as strong as it will go — any employment whatever — and ask whether "in relation to" has to hold the line by itself. Which of the two gives way first, where exactly is the line drawn, and what would we see if the line were in the wrong place?
transcript.author:
**Part one.** Separation case: a defendant who negotiates the gun-for-cocaine swap but leaves the MAC-10 locked in his trunk, or has an associate deliver it — used as barter, never carried. Conversely, passive bearing for protection, with no employment, is carry doing independent work. So both verbs have content under my reading.

Which rivals does this kill? Candidly, almost none. It confirms Scalia's complaint: my "use" is broad enough that most carrying is also use, leaving "carries" thin. But the mirror point cuts his way too — if "use" means weapon-use, carrying a gun for protection is the only independent work, and firing is both. Neither reading dissolves the other. I overstated the "no dichotomy" line.

**Part two.** Push "use" to any employment whatever, and every limit migrates to "in relation to." That prong gives way first — it must, or nothing does. The line sits at purpose or effect: the gun must facilitate, or be intended to facilitate, the drug crime. Blackmun's concurrence flags that even this may be too permissive. If the line sits too low ("during" suffices), every gun-owning drug offender gets five to thirty years; if too high (weapon-use required), Smith's trade escapes and my Part IIA becomes dictum. The parts are load-bearing on each other: my broad "use" is defensible only because "in relation to" gates it. Narrow that gate later, and my barter holding falls with it.

transcript.reader:
Flip it. Had the 1986 Congress added "drug trafficking crime" without meaning to widen "use" at all — the word keeping its weapon sense — would anything in your opinion have read differently? Could the same dictionary entries, the same §924(d) cross-reference, and the same "drugs and guns are dangerous" passage have been assembled to reach the opposite result just as smoothly? If so, name the one piece you would have had to give up.

Now the change list. Which changes does your claim *not* cover: a gun traded for cash later spent on the drugs, a trade only proposed and never completed, a silencer alone rather than a machinegun, a gun that is never the object of the deal at all? And was the line you drew at the indictment — "use" only, "carry" expressly put aside — written down before you looked at the record, or after?
transcript.author:
**1. The counterfactual.** Largely yes — the same materials could be reassembled. The dictionary entries are double-edged: Scalia draws the identical Webster's (2d ed.) to prove ordinary meaning runs the other way. The §924(d) parallel is answerable by his context argument. The “drugs and guns” passage is policy, and policy can justify contraction as easily as expansion; it is rhetoric, not text.

What I would have to give up: the §924(d) structural inference. It is the only piece doing work *beyond* ordinary meaning — the claim that the same word in the same section cannot mean two things. If 1986 merely extended the weapon sense, that inference becomes an accident of drafting, not a command. I would be left with ordinary usage alone — precisely the thin ground I conceded in the previous turn.

**2. What my holding does not reach.**
- *Gun sold for cash later spent on drugs*: not covered. The employment is not with respect to the drug offense; a step removed. My “at a minimum” language leaves it open.
- *Trade proposed, never completed*: covered — that is this case. The charged attempt and conspiracy supply the “during,” and the offer supplies the “in relation to.”
- *Silencer alone*: covered as to “use,” same analysis; §921(a)(3) treats a silencer as a firearm, and the 30-year minimum attaches independently.
- *Gun never the object of the deal, merely present*: not covered. That is carrying or possession, which I expressly reserved.

**3. When I drew the line.** After. The indictment charged only “use,” and I said so. But honoring that reservation was a choice, not a compulsion — and a convenient one: it spared me the carrying question, where my broad “use” would have been surplusage. Principled under our practice of not reaching theories the Government did not plead; self-serving nonetheless. I concede the order.

transcript.reader:
Take the four load-bearing pieces one at a time — the dictionary sense of "use," the §924(d) twin, "in relation to" as "with reference to," and the danger passage. For each, was it forced by something in the case, worked out from the statute with the question in view, or simply written down? And which of the four has never met a case that could have caught it out?

Then the "facilitate, or have the potential of facilitating" gloss. Is that limit held from inside your explanation, or drawn after the fact to keep your broad "use" from swallowing harmless cases? Name the reading — or the case — that would show the line is in the wrong place.
transcript.author:
**The four pieces.**
*Dictionary sense.* Worked out with the question in view — but the move is boilerplate (Perrin). Not forced; Scalia drew the same Webster's to the opposite end. It supplies breadth, not direction.
*§924(d) twin.* Worked out with the question in view, and with the outcome already in mind. I went looking for a second appearance of "use"+"firearm" because ordinary meaning alone wouldn't settle barter. It is the one genuinely constructive step, and the most vulnerable — as I conceded, list those offenses under "involved in" and the inference dies.
*"In relation to" as "with reference to."* Written down. Lifted from the dictionary and from Stewart, Ocampo, Phelps. I said I needn't fix its contours because Smith met any reading — so it carried no weight here.
*Danger passage.* Written down. Advocacy in a judicial register; it would support either breadth or contraction.

Never caught out: the danger passage, because it states nothing falsifiable; the §924(d) twin, because it has never been the ratio anyone litigated.

**The "facilitate, or potential to facilitate" gloss.** Drawn from outside. It comes from Stewart and Ocampo, imported wholesale. My explanation needed a gate on breadth and I borrowed one rather than deriving it; the phrase "potential of facilitating" is especially loose.

The case that shows the line misplaced: *Bailey* — guns locked in a trunk, or a gun used to pry open a drawer, facilitated nothing and were not "use," though the "potential" language would have swept them in. That is the tell: the gloss was doing gatekeeping that belonged to "use" itself.

transcript.reader:
Build the strongest rival properly: the dissent's contextual reading, weapon-use controlled by the 1968 crime-of-violence origin. Name one change — a case, a drafting fact, an edit to §924(d)(3) — that would make the two readings give *different* answers. If nothing can, say plainly whether they are the same explanation at this level, differing only in which way the Court should have gone.

Last, hunt the answer in the starting points. Which of your starting points could I believe *without* already believing the conclusion — and which are just the conclusion under another name, "danger" or "purpose" included? Then strip the machinegun and silencer out: a plain revolver traded for the same cocaine. Does anything in your reading move? If not, name the part that was doing that work.
transcript.author:
**Rival, strongest form.** Scalia: "uses a firearm" means employs it for its distinctive purpose — as a weapon. The 1968 origin in crimes of violence fixes that sense; 1986 added qualifying offenses, not a new meaning of "use." §924(d) cannot control because the phrase takes color from context (his sporting-use example: "use" for lawful sporting purposes is weapon-use, not pawning). Add lenity. It is strong because it treats context, not the dictionary, as decisive — and context is real.

**Separator.** Already present: barter. Cleaner: a gun carried for protection, never displayed, never employed in negotiating the deal. He says "carries" supplies liability; I say "uses" may independently. But plainly, at this level, these are the same *kind* of explanation — ordinary-meaning argument — differing over the generality at which "ordinary" is pitched. The method does not choose between them; only the result differs.

**Starting points.** Independent: the dictionary entries (a fact about language), "ordinary meaning governs," and "same words in the same section bear the same sense" — all statable without my conclusion. Conclusion-laden: the danger passage and "Congress's purpose." I inferred the purpose from my preferred reading, then used it to confirm that reading.

**Revolver.** Nothing moves. Parts (a) and (b) are weapon-agnostic; only the minimum drops from thirty years to five. The MAC-10's features did work in the rhetoric — "currency to cannon," the *Phelps* anecdote — not in the analysis. That is the tell that the danger passage was decoration.

report:
# Report: Smith v. United States, §924(c)(1) ("uses a firearm")

## 1. The question, frozen

What counts as "uses a firearm" under 18 U.S.C. §924(c)(1)? Range: guns employed in connection with a drug trafficking crime, on these facts (a proposed MAC-10-for-cocaine swap). Kind of question: what counts as what under a rule. The owner sharpens it himself: not "use" alone, but "use" *during and in relation to* a drug crime — barter, collateral, bludgeon yes; coincidental or innocent handling no.

One limit, drawn after the record was read: the Court refuses to reach "carries" because the indictment charged only "use." The owner concedes this order and calls the refusal convenient.

## 2. The claim in parts, with jobs

**Parts.** P1 "Use" takes its ordinary broad sense (to convert to one's service). P2 The same phrase in §924(d)(3) covers guns intended for sale or trade, so the same word in §924(c)(1) covers barter. P3 "In relation to" means "with reference to"; at minimum the gun must facilitate, or have the potential to facilitate, the drug crime. P4 Guns entering drug deals heighten danger; Congress meant to reach this. P5 "As a weapon" appears nowhere in the text, so no such requirement. P6 The broad "use" leaves no odd gap beside "carries."

**Jobs.** J1 barter counts (given, from the case); J2 shooting, brandishing and pistol-whipping count (given — no court disputes it); J3 §924(c)(1) and §924(d) read the word alike (the owner's own move); J4 head-scratching and coincidental possession are excluded (given — his gate, and Blackmun's caution); J5 "carries" still does independent work (added by me); J6 a gun sold for cash later spent on drugs is excluded (added by the owner in this conversation).

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Because |
|---|---|---|
| P1 dictionary sense of "use" | **Loose** | The dissent draws the same Webster's entry to the opposite end. Swapping in "use for its intended purpose" works as well for *its* side. P1 supplies breadth, not direction. |
| P2 §924(d)(3) twin | **Held if** | Held only by the job that Congress listed commerce offenses under "intended to be used." Swap that phrase for the neighbouring "involved in," which Congress used two lines away, and the inference dies — the owner says so. That job has never been tested. What would settle it: the 1986 drafting history. |
| P3 "in relation to" / "potential of facilitating" | **Borrowed** | Lifted wholesale from *Stewart*, *Ocampo*, *Phelps*. It rests on a line of circuit cases not tested here. It also carried no weight in this case: the owner says Smith met any reading. |
| P4 danger and purpose passage | **Idle** | Change the gun to a plain revolver and nothing in the reasoning moves; only the minimum drops from thirty years to five. The passage would support either result. The owner calls it decoration. |
| P5 "as a weapon" is absent from the text | **Loose** | A silence can be read either way. The owner himself allows the space is near binary: one reading counts commodity, the other does not. |
| P6 "no strange dichotomy" with "carries" | **Loose** | The owner withdrew it here. Scalia's dichotomy does as well, arguably better: the two verbs overlap under the broad reading. |
| "Use only, not carry" limit on the range | **Fixed** | The owner set it and did not test it; he concedes he drew it after reading the record. |

## 4. Whole-claim checks

**Flip.** The owner concedes that the same materials — the same dictionary, an answerable §924(d) argument, the same policy passage — would have been assembled to reach the opposite result just as smoothly. Exactly one piece would have to be surrendered: P2. That makes P2 the whole load-bearing wall.

**Answer hidden in the starting points.** The danger-and-purpose passage is the conclusion under another name: the owner says he inferred Congress's purpose from his preferred reading, then used that purpose to confirm the reading. Taking P4 away removes support; it does not decide the case either way.

**Pairs that pull.** Push "use" to any employment whatever and every limit migrates to "in relation to." That gate gives way first, and the owner agrees it must. Narrow the gate later — as *Bailey* did — and the barter holding falls with it. J5 pulls the same way: make "use" broad and "carries" goes thin.

**Catch-all and gauge.** "Potential of facilitating" is the catch-all, and no gauge comes with it — nothing measurable that would show it swallowing jobs it should not. *Bailey* is the showing that it did. The owner's own verdict: the gatekeeping belonged to "use" itself.

**What the change list leaves out.** A gun sold for cash later spent on drugs; a gun merely present during the deal; a gun pledged as collateral (which the owner says counts but no court has tested); the fact that the trade was never completed. These are stated limits, mostly said aloud — but the "use-only" limit was set after looking.

**Direction.** This is a rule question, not a cause question, so reverse does not bite. No confusion of a reading with the thing read.

**The rival.** Scalia's contextual reading — weapon-use, fixed by the 1968 crime-of-violence origin, with §924(d) taking colour from its own context — is fully built. The owner grants that at this level the two are the same *kind* of explanation, ordinary-meaning arguments pitched at different generality. No change on the list separates them on these facts. The offered separator — a gun carried for protection, never employed — is a finer question, and is recorded as new.

**Where the parts came from.** P1 built, but boilerplate. P2 built with the outcome in view, criticised, and exposed — the one constructive step, and the most fragile. P3 asserted and imported. P4 asserted rhetoric.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

One or two jobs, not more. First, give P2 an independent hold: a drafting source showing what the 1986 Congress meant by listing commerce offenses under "intended to be used," written down before looking. Second, test the gate: take a case where "use" and "in relation to" must come apart — a gun pledged as collateral for a drug debt, the owner's own example — and say in advance what the gate does there and what would show the line misplaced.

## 6. What this does not show

Hard to vary is not true. P1 may be right and still loose; the dissent's reading may be wrong and still tightly held. This report finds which parts are pinned, which are free, and what would pin them.

## 7. One next step

Charge the same facts under "carries" alone and run both readings on that case. That is the change the Court expressly declined to face, and it is where the two explanations are most likely to come apart.
